direct_observables: temperature rise ΔT of calorimeter cell following electrical energy input
electrical energy Q dissipated by heater (from voltage, current, and time)
equilibrium temperature before and after heating pulse
derived_observables: isobaric heat capacity Cp = Q/(n × ΔT)
specific heat capacity cp = Q/(m × ΔT)
enthalpy increment H(T2) − H(T1) from cumulative heating pulses
phase transition temperature from Cp anomaly
enthalpy of transition ΔtrsH from integration of Cp peak
supported_sample_types: thin films and coatings (scraped or peeled off substrate)
synthetic products available in small quantity
unsupported_sample_types: gases (no containment in standard small adiabatic cells)
highly volatile liquids without sealed cells
samples requiring more than ~1 g for representative measurement
extremely corrosive materials that attack gold or copper cells
strongly exothermic mixtures that could run away thermally
typical_output_formats: Cp vs. T tabulation at discrete temperature points
smoothed Cp(T) polynomial or spline curves
Cp anomaly peak for phase transitions

constraints.hard_limits: lower limit set by cryostat base temperature (~1.8 K with pumped 4He, ~0.5 K with 3He); upper limit set by radiation heat leak becoming unmanageable above ~400–500 K for small cells
constraints.notes: most published work covers 5–350 K; some specialized setups reach 500 K

constraints.hard_limits: minimum ~10 mg (limited by addenda-to-sample ratio); maximum 1 g by definition of this technique category
constraints.notes: optimal range 100–500 mg balances signal-to-noise against material availability

constraints.hard_limits: must produce ΔT of 0.5–3 K; energy must not overshoot adiabatic shield tracking
constraints.notes: smaller pulses near phase transitions to resolve Cp anomalies; larger pulses in featureless regions for throughput

constraints.hard_limits: reduced to 0.1–0.5 K near phase transitions for adequate resolution
constraints.notes: total measurement time scales inversely with step size; ~100–300 points per full temperature scan

constraints.hard_limits: must wait until drift rate < 0.01–0.05 mK/s before next heating pulse
constraints.notes: longer equilibration needed near phase transitions and at lowest temperatures

constraints.hard_limits: pressure must be low enough to suppress gas conduction between cell and shield
constraints.notes: helium exchange gas used for initial cooldown, then pumped out before measurement

variables.name: temperature
variables.typical_values: 5 K to 400 K in 0.5–3 K steps
variables.effect: temperature scan maps out Cp(T) revealing phase transitions, Debye behavior at low T, and classical limit at high T

variables.name: electrical_heating_energy
variables.effect: determines ΔT per point; adjusted to maintain ΔT in the 0.5–3 K range across the temperature span

variables.name: pressure
variables.role: usually fixed at ambient or under vacuum
variables.typical_values: sealed cell at ~0.1 MPa or evacuated
variables.effect: measurements typically isobaric at atmospheric pressure inside sealed cell; surrounding vacuum provides adiabatic isolation

instrument_components: miniature calorimeter cell — thin-walled gold, copper, or silver vessel (0.5–3 cm³ volume) with low thermal mass, typically 0.5–2 g empty
resistance heater — manganin or constantan wire wound noninductively around or cemented to calorimeter cell; known resistance to ±0.01%
precision thermometer — platinum resistance thermometer (PRT), germanium resistance thermometer (GRT, for T < 30 K), or calibrated Cernox sensor
adiabatic shield — gold-plated copper shield surrounding cell, equipped with its own heater and thermometer, PID-controlled to track cell temperature within ±0.1–1 mK
outer guard shield — second thermal shield to reduce radiation load on adiabatic shield
cryostat — liquid helium or closed-cycle refrigerator providing base temperatures of 1.8–5 K
precision current source — supplies known DC current to cell heater for energy input measurement
precision voltmeter — measures heater voltage drop for energy Q = ∫V·I·dt
digital timer — synchronizes heater on/off with µs precision
resistance bridge or AC lock-in system — reads thermometer resistance with resolution better than 1 part in 10⁶
vacuum system — diffusion or turbomolecular pump achieving <10⁻³ Pa around calorimeter
data acquisition computer — logs T, V, I, time; automates heating-equilibration-measurement cycle
environmental_requirements: high vacuum (<10⁻³ Pa) surrounding calorimeter cell to eliminate gas conduction
vibration-isolated optical table or heavy platform to prevent microphonic noise in thermometer readings
temperature-stable laboratory (±1 °C) to avoid drift in electronics and cryostat performance
electromagnetic shielding (Faraday cage) for low-noise resistance thermometry
helium gas handling system for cooldown and cryostat operation

geometry: granular, powder, or small pieces that pack into miniature calorimeter cell
pressed pellet for improved thermal contact
thin disk or wafer for uniform thermal equilibration
sample_requirements.size_limits: 10 mg to 1000 mg (1 g); optimal 50–500 mg; total cell + sample mass typically 2–5 g
sample_requirements.thickness_limits: individual pieces should be <3 mm to ensure rapid internal thermal equilibration; finer granularity preferred
surface_requirements: clean, oxide-free surface for good thermal contact with cell walls
mounting_requirements: sample loaded into calorimeter cell with good packing to maximize thermal contact
small amount of helium exchange gas (~5 kPa at room temperature) sealed inside cell to ensure internal thermal equilibration
cell sealed with indium gasket, solder, or epoxy depending on temperature range
cell mounted on thin nylon or silk threads to minimize heat leak to adiabatic shield
preparation_requirements: accurate mass determination on microbalance (±0.01 mg)
purity verification (DSC screening, elemental analysis, or spectroscopic check)
drying under vacuum or inert gas for hygroscopic materials
degassing at moderate temperature under vacuum for porous or high-surface-area samples
molar mass must be known for converting specific Cp to molar Cp

calibration_requirements: empty-cell (addenda) heat capacity measurement over full temperature range — critical because addenda is a large fraction of total signal for small samples
thermometer calibration against ITS-90 fixed points or calibrated reference thermometer
heater resistance measurement as a function of temperature (for accurate energy determination)
electrical calibration check: verify Q = V × I × t against precision standards
adiabatic shield PID tuning verification — shield must track cell temperature to within specified tolerance
validation run with standard reference material (sapphire or copper) to confirm overall accuracy
reference_materials: synthetic sapphire (α-Al2O3) — NIST SRM 720, primary Cp standard from 10 K to 2250 K
high-purity copper (99.999%) — well-characterized Cp, especially useful below 300 K
benzoic acid — calorimetric standard for energy calibration and Cp verification
n-heptane — liquid standard with well-known Cp
NIST SRM 2232 (indium) — temperature and enthalpy of fusion standard
consumables: indium wire or gasket for cell sealing (~0.5 mm diameter)
Apiezon N grease for thermal contact where applicable
high-purity helium gas for exchange gas and cryostat operation
liquid helium or compressed helium for closed-cycle cryocooler
liquid nitrogen for radiation shield cooling
safety_notes: cryogenic liquid handling: frostbite risk, oxygen displacement in enclosed spaces — use proper ventilation and PPE
high vacuum systems: implosion hazard — ensure proper shielding on glass dewars
electrical safety: precision current sources can deliver sustained current — follow lockout/tagout procedures during cell loading
sealed calorimeter cells under helium pressure — risk of rupture if overheated; do not exceed design temperature

performance.sensitivity: capable of resolving heat capacity contributions as small as ~50 µJ/K for a well-constructed miniature calorimeter; total Cp of cell + sample typically 0.5–5 J/K
performance.detection_limit: minimum practical sample mass ~10 mg, limited by addenda-to-sample Cp ratio; sample Cp should be at least 10–20% of total (cell + sample) Cp

resolution.temporal: not applicable (equilibrium method; each data point requires 5–30 min)
resolution.energy: energy input resolution ~0.01% from precision voltage/current/time measurement

performance.dynamic_range: Cp from ~0.001 J/(g·K) at cryogenic temperatures to ~5 J/(g·K) for liquids near room temperature
performance.accuracy: 0.3–1% for Cp in favorable cases (100–500 mg sample, 50–350 K); degrades to 1–3% below 10 K and above 400 K due to increased addenda fraction and radiation leaks
performance.precision: 0.1–0.3% repeatability at a given temperature point
performance.throughput: single sample per run; one complete temperature scan (5–400 K) requires 3–7 days of continuous operation
performance.measurement_speed: one Cp data point every 10–30 minutes (heating pulse + equilibration); ~50–200 points per day

data_and_interpretation.raw_signal_type: thermometer resistance (converted to temperature via calibration polynomial) recorded before and after each discrete electrical heating pulse of known energy Q = V × I × Δt
preprocessing_steps: convert thermometer resistance to temperature using ITS-90 calibration curve
determine equilibrium temperatures T1 (before pulse) and T2 (after pulse) by extrapolating pre-drift and post-drift to midpoint of heating period (Regnault–Pfaundler correction)
calculate gross heat capacity: Cp,gross = Q / (T2 − T1)
subtract addenda (empty cell) heat capacity at the midpoint temperature: Cp,sample = Cp,gross − Cp,addenda
apply curvature correction if ΔT is large and Cp varies significantly over the interval
correct for heat exchange (temperature drift) during heating period using pre- and post-drift rates
analysis_methods: point-by-point Cp determination: Cp at Tmid = (T1 + T2)/2 from each heating pulse
polynomial or spline smoothing of Cp(T) data for thermodynamic table generation
Debye T³ extrapolation of Cp below lowest measured temperature to T → 0
integration ∫Cp dT to obtain enthalpy increments H(T) − H(0)
integration ∫(Cp/T) dT to obtain standard entropy S°(T)
peak integration of Cp anomaly to determine transition enthalpy ΔtrsH
lattice Cp fitting (Debye or Einstein models) to separate lattice and excess contributions
model_assumptions: thermal equilibrium is achieved before and after each heating pulse (drift rate criterion satisfied)
sample is isothermal throughout its volume during equilibrium periods (internal thermal relaxation << equilibration wait time)
adiabatic conditions are maintained during heating pulse: no net heat exchange with shield (shield tracks cell temperature perfectly)
electrical energy delivered to heater is entirely converted to heat within the calorimeter cell (no energy loss through leads)
addenda heat capacity is stable and reproducible between empty-cell run and sample run
helium exchange gas inside cell provides sufficient thermal coupling between sample and cell wall
fit_parameters: heat capacity Cp at each midpoint temperature Tmid
pre-drift and post-drift rates (dT/dt) for drift correction
Debye temperature θD (from low-T Cp fitting: Cp ∝ T³)
polynomial coefficients for smooth Cp(T) representation
transition temperature Ttrs and enthalpy ΔtrsH from peak analysis
common_artifacts: addenda overcorrection: if empty-cell Cp changes between runs (e.g., grease aging, oxidation of cell), the subtracted addenda is wrong, producing systematic Cp offset
heat leak artifact: imperfect adiabatic shield tracking causes temperature-dependent systematic error that appears as a smooth Cp bias
exchange gas artifact: if sealed helium pressure is too high, gas Cp contributes a measurable addendum not captured in empty-cell run (especially above 200 K where gas Cp is nontrivial)
pre-melting artifact: near a solid–liquid transition, anomalous Cp rise due to impurity-induced pre-melting can be mistaken for an intrinsic anomaly
radiation leak artifact: above ~350 K, radiative heat exchange between cell and shield grows as T⁴, causing apparent Cp increase if not corrected
quality_control_checks: verify Cp of reference material (sapphire or copper) agrees with literature values within stated accuracy over full temperature range
check that pre-drift and post-drift rates are acceptably small (<0.05 mK/s) before accepting each data point
compare heating and cooling direction scans to check for hysteresis or irreversibility
check consistency of addenda subtraction by running two addenda measurements and comparing
verify that ΔT per point is consistent with smooth Cp(T) curve (no outlier jumps indicating heater or sensor malfunction)
confirm that ∫(Cp/T)dT from 0 to 298.15 K gives S°(298.15 K) consistent with other literature sources
failure_modes: loss of vacuum: gas conduction between cell and shield destroys adiabatic condition; Cp data becomes unreliable
adiabatic shield controller failure or oscillation: shield temperature deviates from cell, causing large heat leaks
thermometer calibration drift: systematic temperature offset accumulates over long measurement campaigns
cell seal failure: loss of helium exchange gas inside cell causes poor internal thermal equilibration; manifested as sluggish equilibration and scatter in Cp
sample decomposition: irreversible Cp changes upon heating indicate chemical degradation
heater break or short: abrupt change in heater resistance invalidates energy calibration

uncertainty.level: typical combined standard uncertainty 0.3–1% for Cp in optimal conditions (100–500 mg, 20–350 K); 1–3% at extremes of temperature range or for very small (<50 mg) samples
random_sources: thermometer noise and resolution (Johnson noise, digitization)
residual temperature drift during equilibration (imperfect extrapolation to midpoint)
electrical measurement noise in heater voltage and current
vibration-induced microphonic signals in thermometer leads
statistical scatter in repeated measurements at same temperature
systematic_sources: addenda subtraction uncertainty — dominant for small samples where addenda may be 50–90% of total Cp
heat exchange correction — residual uncompensated heat leak through adiabatic shield imperfections
thermometer calibration uncertainty — propagates directly to temperature scale
heater energy calibration — uncertainty in V, I, and timing
exchange gas correction — Cp of helium gas inside cell may not be fully captured in addenda
sample mass uncertainty — ±0.01 mg on a 100 mg sample is 0.01%, negligible, but impurity mass contributes to error in moles
curvature correction — uncertainty when Cp changes rapidly within a single ΔT step
radiation heat leak — grows as T⁴ and is difficult to correct precisely above 350 K
uncertainty.operator_dependence: moderate — sample loading, cell sealing quality, exchange gas pressure, and adiabatic shield tuning are operator-dependent; experienced operators achieve significantly better addenda reproducibility
uncertainty.model_dependence: low to moderate — the fundamental measurement is a direct ratio Q/ΔT, but corrections for drift, addenda, and curvature introduce model dependence; Debye extrapolation to T → 0 adds additional model dependence to integrated S° values
dominant_error_sources: addenda subtraction (especially for samples <100 mg where cell Cp dominates)
adiabatic shield heat leak correction (worst at low and high temperature extremes)
Debye T³ extrapolation uncertainty when lowest measured temperature is >8 K
reported_as: combined expanded uncertainty U(Cp) at 95% confidence level (k = 2)
relative uncertainty as percentage of Cp
point-by-point uncertainty from propagation of V, I, Δt, ΔT, and addenda uncertainties

description_block.technique_overview: Small-sample adiabatic calorimetry is a precision thermal measurement technique designed to determine the heat capacity Cp of samples with masses below 1 gram, typically in the 50–500 mg range. It operates on the same fundamental principle as standard adiabatic calorimetry — delivering a known quantity of electrical energy to a thermally isolated sample and measuring the resulting temperature rise — but employs a miniaturized calorimeter cell with reduced thermal mass to maintain an acceptable ratio of sample signal to addenda (empty-cell) background. Developed to address the need for thermodynamic data on scarce, expensive, or difficult-to-synthesize materials, this technique achieves accuracies of 0.3–1% for Cp across a typical temperature range of 5–400 K, making it only slightly less accurate than full-size adiabatic calorimetry while requiring one to two orders of magnitude less material.
description_block.how_it_operates: The sample is loaded into a small thin-walled calorimeter cell (typically gold, copper, or silver, with empty mass 0.5–2 g and volume 0.5–3 cm³) together with a small amount of helium exchange gas to ensure internal thermal equilibrium. The sealed cell is mounted on thin threads inside a gold-plated adiabatic shield, which is itself enclosed within an outer guard shield, all housed in a cryostat under high vacuum (<10⁻³ Pa). A precision resistance heater wound around or cemented to the cell delivers a measured electrical energy pulse Q = V × I × Δt, and a calibrated thermometer (platinum or germanium resistance thermometer, or Cernox sensor) records the temperature before and after the pulse. The adiabatic shield is actively controlled via PID feedback to track the cell temperature within ±0.1–1 mK throughout the measurement, ensuring negligible heat exchange between cell and surroundings. After each heating pulse, the system is allowed to reach thermal equilibrium (drift rate < 0.05 mK/s), and the equilibrium temperature is determined by extrapolating the pre-drift and post-drift traces to the midpoint of the heating period.
description_block.core_theory: The fundamental relation is Cp = Q/(n × ΔT), where Q is the electrical energy input (joules), n is the amount of substance (moles), and ΔT = T₂ − T₁ is the temperature rise between equilibrium states. Because the measurement is performed under adiabatic conditions (no heat exchange with surroundings), all energy delivered by the heater raises the temperature of the calorimeter cell plus sample: Cp,total = Q/ΔT, and Cp,sample = Cp,total − Cp,addenda. The addenda contribution from the miniature cell, heater, thermometer, and sealed helium gas is determined in a separate empty-cell measurement. For small samples, the addenda-to-sample Cp ratio is the critical figure of merit: ratios above 5:1 degrade accuracy significantly because the sample Cp is obtained as a small difference of two large numbers. The curvature correction accounts for the nonlinear variation of Cp within the finite interval ΔT, typically implemented as a second-order Taylor expansion. At the lowest temperatures (below ~10 K), Cp follows the Debye T³ law for insulators or a γT + βT³ form for metals, enabling extrapolation to absolute zero for entropy calculations.
description_block.setup: A typical small-sample adiabatic calorimeter comprises: (1) a miniature calorimeter cell machined from high-purity gold or copper, with thin walls (0.2–0.5 mm) and a volume of 0.5–3 cm³, sealed with an indium O-ring or soft-solder joint; (2) a manganin or constantan wire heater (50–500 Ω) wound bifilarly around the cell exterior and cemented with GE varnish or Stycast epoxy for good thermal contact; (3) a calibrated thermometer — a capsule-type platinum resistance thermometer for T > 30 K and a germanium resistance thermometer for T < 30 K, or a single Cernox sensor covering the full range; (4) a gold-plated copper adiabatic shield (inner shield) with its own heater and thermometer, PID-controlled to track the cell temperature; (5) an outer guard shield to intercept radiation from the cryostat walls; (6) a liquid-helium cryostat or closed-cycle refrigerator providing base temperatures down to 1.8–5 K; (7) a high-vacuum system (<10⁻³ Pa); and (8) precision electronics including a DC current source, nanovoltmeter, AC resistance bridge, and a computer for automated data acquisition and shield control. The cell is suspended inside the adiabatic shield on thin nylon or silk threads to minimize conductive heat leaks.
description_block.suitable_for: This technique is specifically designed for samples that are available only in limited quantities — typically expensive synthetic compounds, isotopically enriched materials, newly discovered phases, pharmaceutical actives, or samples from difficult high-pressure or high-temperature syntheses. It is the method of choice when authoritative heat capacity data from 5 to 400 K are needed but fewer than 500 mg of material can be spared. Common applications include: determining standard molar heat capacities and deriving standard entropies S°(298.15 K) for thermodynamic tables; characterizing solid-state phase transitions (order–disorder, magnetic, structural); measuring the electronic heat capacity coefficient γ in metals and superconductors; studying glass transitions in amorphous pharmaceuticals and polymers; and providing Cp data for rare-earth compounds, intermetallics, and advanced functional materials. The technique is also used as a complement to DSC when higher absolute accuracy is required for small sample quantities.
description_block.core_limitations: The principal limitation is the unfavorable addenda-to-sample ratio inherent in using a miniaturized cell with a sample mass below 1 g. Even with a carefully minimized cell (0.5–2 g empty), the addenda heat capacity can constitute 50–90% of the total measured Cp at some temperatures, amplifying the uncertainty in the addenda subtraction. This limits achievable accuracy to 0.3–1%, compared to 0.05–0.3% for standard adiabatic calorimetry with 5–30 g samples. The temperature range is typically restricted to 5–400 K because radiation heat exchange (scaling as T⁴) becomes difficult to manage above ~400 K with small cells that have limited surface treatment options. Below 5 K, the total Cp of cell plus sample becomes very small and the signal-to-noise ratio deteriorates. Measurements are inherently slow — a full 5–400 K scan requires 3–7 days — and only one sample is measured per run. Sample preparation requires careful mass determination and purity assessment, and the loading/sealing process for the miniature cell demands manual dexterity and experience.
description_block.sample_preparation: The sample is first verified for identity and purity by complementary methods (DSC, XRD, spectroscopy, or elemental analysis). It is then dried under vacuum or inert gas flow if hygroscopic, and degassed at moderate temperature under vacuum if porous or high-surface-area. The sample mass is determined to ±0.01 mg on an analytical microbalance; for conversion to molar quantities, the molar mass must be accurately known. The sample is loaded as a powder, small granules, or a pressed pellet into the pre-weighed miniature calorimeter cell. Approximately 5 kPa (at room temperature) of high-purity helium gas is introduced into the cell as an exchange gas before sealing to ensure thermal equilibrium between sample and cell wall during measurement. The cell is sealed with an indium gasket, soft solder, or low-temperature epoxy, and weighed again to confirm sample mass and verify seal integrity. For air-sensitive samples, all loading and sealing operations are performed in an inert-atmosphere glove box.
description_block.calibration_and_references: Calibration is performed at three levels: (1) Thermometer calibration — the resistance thermometer is calibrated against ITS-90 fixed points (superconducting transition temperatures of reference metals, triple points of hydrogen, neon, argon, mercury, and water) or against a reference thermometer traceable to national standards, yielding a calibration polynomial R(T). (2) Addenda determination — the empty calorimeter cell (with heater, thermometer, thermal grease, and sealed helium gas) is measured over the full temperature range under identical conditions to the subsequent sample measurement; this addenda Cp(T) curve is subtracted point by point. (3) Validation with a certified reference — a known mass of synthetic sapphire (α-Al₂O₃, NIST SRM 720) or high-purity copper is measured and the resulting Cp compared with certified values to verify the accuracy of the entire measurement chain. Agreement within ±0.5% for sapphire confirms proper operation. The addenda measurement should be repeated whenever the cell is disassembled or the internal grease/varnish configuration is altered.
description_block.data_interpretation: Each raw data point consists of an equilibrium temperature T₁ before a heating pulse, the electrical energy Q delivered during the pulse, and the equilibrium temperature T₂ afterward. The gross heat capacity is Cp,gross = Q/(T₂ − T₁) at the midpoint temperature Tmid = (T₁ + T₂)/2. The sample heat capacity is obtained by subtracting the addenda: Cp,sample(Tmid) = Cp,gross(Tmid) − Cp,addenda(Tmid), where the addenda are interpolated from the smooth empty-cell curve. A curvature correction is applied when Cp changes significantly over the ΔT interval. The resulting Cp(T) data are fitted to polynomial or spline functions for tabulation. Standard entropy is obtained by integrating S°(T) = ∫₀ᵀ (Cp/T)dT, with the segment from 0 to the lowest measured temperature evaluated using a Debye T³ extrapolation (Cp = aT³) for insulators or a γT + βT³ model for metals. Phase transition enthalpies are determined by integrating the anomalous Cp above a baseline representing the lattice contribution. Smoothed Cp(T) and derived H(T) and S°(T) are reported in tabular form at rounded temperature intervals.
description_block.common_pitfalls: The most consequential pitfall is inaccurate addenda subtraction. Because the empty-cell heat capacity is a large fraction of the total, even a 0.5% error in the addenda propagates to a much larger relative error in the derived sample Cp — for a 100 mg sample with an addenda-to-sample ratio of 4:1, a 0.5% addenda error becomes a 2.5% error in sample Cp. Other common pitfalls include: insufficient exchange gas inside the cell, which results in slow internal equilibration and anomalously scattered Cp data; poor vacuum around the cell, which introduces gas conduction and invalidates the adiabatic assumption; degradation of the adiabatic shield tracking at temperature extremes (very low T where electronic noise dominates, or high T where radiation leaks are severe); using temperature steps that are too large near phase transitions, causing the transition to be poorly resolved or the curvature correction to be inadequate; and neglecting to verify sample purity, which can introduce pre-melting artifacts that distort the Cp curve near the melting point.
description_block.artifacts_and_failure_modes: The dominant artifact is the heat leak error: if the adiabatic shield does not perfectly track the cell temperature, a systematic temperature-dependent bias appears in Cp. Positive drift (cell warming faster than equilibrium) causes Cp to be overestimated, and negative drift causes underestimation. The magnitude of this artifact scales with drift rate and the thermal conductance of the cell-to-shield link. The radiation heat exchange artifact becomes significant above ~350 K, where T⁴ radiation between cell and shield surfaces that are not perfectly temperature-matched produces a spurious Cp contribution that increases steeply with temperature. The exchange gas artifact occurs if the sealed helium gas inside the cell has a different pressure than assumed in the addenda run, adding or subtracting a small temperature-dependent Cp offset. Pre-melting artifacts appear as an anomalous Cp rise 1–20 K below the melting point of impure samples, caused by eutectic impurity melting. Failure modes include: vacuum leak causing loss of adiabatic isolation; thermometer calibration drift after thermal cycling; heater wire break or short-circuit producing incorrect energy values; and cell seal failure releasing exchange gas, evidenced by dramatically increased equilibration times.
description_block.reporting_checklist: Published results from small-sample adiabatic calorimetry should include: sample provenance, purity, and characterization method; sample mass and molar mass used for molar Cp conversion; calorimeter cell material and empty mass; temperature range measured; number of data points and typical ΔT step sizes; addenda-to-sample Cp ratio at representative temperatures; addenda subtraction method and reproducibility; thermometer type and calibration traceability; validation results against reference material (sapphire or copper); method of Debye extrapolation below lowest measured temperature and the temperature range used for the fit; smoothing procedure applied to Cp(T); tabulated Cp, H(T) − H(0), and S°(T) − S°(0) at standard temperature intervals; combined expanded uncertainty U(Cp) at 95% confidence level (k = 2) with a breakdown of major uncertainty components; and any phase transitions observed with Ttrs and ΔtrsH values. For ThermoML encoding, Cp values are stored with nCombExpandUncertValue at the 95% confidence level.
